On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram is Udayaditya’s subordinate guard: he obeys the prince’s command to open the door but insists that he cannot let him leave, so Udayaditya disarms and binds him before escaping. On the night of Udayaditya’s escape, their roles are reversed: Sitaram himself opens the prison, seizes Udayaditya, carries him out under the pretext of saving him from the fire, and guides the now-confined and helpless prince to safety.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathan assassins to kill Basanta Ray when he stopped at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. That attempt failed when one Pathan’s brother lured Basanta Ray’s retainers away, but the Pathan himself could not bring himself to kill him.

The old king’s life finally ended when Pratapaditya issued a written death sentence. Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers entered Raigarh in disguise, confronted Basanta Ray during his evening prayers, and Abdul killed him with a sword.
In the palace’s inner quarters, disguised as a woman; and later in the king’s room, appearing as himself as the jester Ramai Bhand.
Mangala secretly prepares and administers a ritual poison, causing Surma to ingest it and die rather than leave for her father’s house.
The king remarries, leaving Vibha without a place in her husband’s palace; when she finally arrives, her hopes of happiness are shattered.

Rukmini tricks Udayaditya into giving her his ring, which bears the Yubaraj’s name and seal. Sitaram and Bhagavat use that seal to stamp a forged petition accusing Udayaditya of treason and seeking the kingdom from the Emperor. Bhagavat then presents it to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted it from an escaped servant of Udayaditya. Although Pratapaditya admits he does not fully believe the accusation, he treats the petition—and the ring’s seal as apparent authentication—as sufficient justification to imprison Udayaditya and have him watched so he cannot act secretly.

Ramchandra Ray’s escape required Udayaditya to defy Pratapaditya’s orders and use force to break out of the palace, making Pratapaditya pay closer attention to his son. Consequently, when Udayaditya supported the dismissed guards, Sitaram and Bhagavat, Pratapaditya quickly learned of it and forbade anyone from helping them. Surma secretly continued sending them stipends through a maid, but Mangala revealed this. Pratapaditya therefore ordered Surma sent to her father’s home. When she refused, he threatened to imprison Udayaditya, forcing Surma to leave.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s grief at being left behind by those he loves: the joy and companionship of the past have vanished, leaving him alone amid emptiness, unable to find the spirit to continue living.

He sings it first at sunset in Raigarh, alone and reflecting on his absent loved ones and the broken strings of his sitar. He sings it again in Jessore, slowly while holding Vibha’s hand, after finding the once-joyful household silent, dark, and deserted.

Rukmini failed to prevent Udayaditya and Basanta Ray from escaping by boat, and Udayaditya consequently reached Raigarh. She then alerted Pratapaditya that Udayaditya had escaped with Basanta Ray and helped the soldiers locate him. Pratapaditya responded by ordering Muktiyar Khan to capture Udayaditya and execute Basanta Ray if he was found. Although Udayaditya surrendered, Muktiyar carried out the separate death order against Basanta Ray, who was killed in Raigarh.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra with cool indifference, barely acknowledging him and treating him as an incidental presence while attending to official business. Later, in Ramchandra’s own court, Ramchandra reverses the hierarchy: he presents Pratapaditya as inferior, allows his courtiers to ridicule him, and regards even marrying Pratapaditya’s daughter as an act that enhances Pratapaditya’s family rather than his own.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore, where she befriends the palace servants and secretly follows everything happening there. When the Rajmahishi seeks a way to separate Surma from Udayaditya, Mangala prepares a ritualized poison, which Surma takes and dies from.

After Surma’s death, Mangala conspires with Sitaram and enters Udayaditya’s chamber during a storm. He briefly mistakes her for Surma, but she then accuses him of ruining her and claims that she wants only his love. Exploiting his guilt and grief, she obtains his ring, while planning to regain control over him and the palace through her spells and manipulation.

Udayaditya’s early lament grows from his conviction that he is too weak and unsuited to rule, and that royal expectations have brought misery to himself and Surma. After the catastrophe caused by his weakness, he concludes that he has brought ruin upon others and declares that he will leave the world. When brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he therefore admits he is unworthy of the kingdom, asks to be released from the throne, and vows before Ma-Kali never to rule Jessore, touch its scepter, or claim even an iota of its territory. He formally gives the succession to Samaraditya and asks only to depart for Kashi, where he will live apart and establish a guest house and temple.

Ramchandra Ray, wounded in his pride, wrote to Pratapaditya declaring that he had renounced Vibha and forbidding her return to Chandradwip. Rammohan refused to carry it, so the old Nayanchand took it instead. Afraid of Pratapaditya’s reaction, Nayanchand handed it to the Mahishi, who concealed its true contents. When Basanta Ray read it, he advised her to send Vibha back immediately and to announce that Ramchandra had written asking for her return. The Mahishi therefore told Vibha—and the household—that the letter was a loving summons to Chandradwip, filling Vibha with joy and restoring her faith in her husband.

Pratapaditya had the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal-wood logs, expecting Ramchandra Ray’s boat to be trapped. However, Rammohan and the others hauled the boat over the logs and continued down the canal. The guards could neither shoot them nor pursue promptly: they lacked a usable gun and ammunition, and the boat sent after them was delayed until escape was impossible.

Basanta Ray’s sitar is his “eternal companion,” closely tied to his love, music, and happiness with those dear to him. When he must leave Udayaditya, he tries to play it furiously, but his tears disrupt him; he finally leaves it behind, declaring that he will never play it again. Later, with Udayaditya imprisoned, he says the sitar’s strings have broken and can no longer be tuned. Its silence and brokenness mirror his own shattered joy: music still rises within him, but the people he played for are gone, leaving him feeling utterly alone and unable to go on.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for fearlessly involving himself in his subjects’ affairs and opposing oppression, even against his father’s wishes. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya overwhelms him: he hesitates, abandons plans to defend the oppressed, flees rather than stopping an official’s beating, and cannot bring himself to provide financial help to suffering subjects.
He arranges a fire near the prison, exploiting the guards’ distraction to release Udayaditya and lead him out into the open, thereby undoing the imprisonment caused by the forged petition.

On the first occasion, Rammohan rescues Ramchandra Ray by escaping through the palace roof: he ties sheets into a rope, carries the king down on his back, lowers him into the boat, and jumps down after him.

On the second, after Vibha is humiliated and faints, Rammohan throws the insulting jester out by the scruff of his neck, lifts Vibha himself, carries her from the palace, and places her in a palanquin before returning to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as a princess receiving her royal son-in-law: the Mahishi loads her with thick gold bangles, diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle. She is shy, radiant, and unable to hide her joyful excitement.

In Chandradwip, she deliberately abandons that royal presentation. She refuses a palanquin, dresses like a common woman—“like a beggar-woman”—and goes on foot to seek Ramchandra. Her veil slips, she is mistaken for a beggar or maidservant, and she approaches him humbly, falling at his feet in grief rather than appearing as his queen.

After Surma’s death, the bedchamber window becomes a place of absence and longing: Udayaditya sits where Surma once sat, looking at the familiar moonlight and garden while hoping, despite knowing it is impossible, that she will return. In the prison, the small window becomes a symbol of freedom and hope. Through its view of the sky and flying birds, he imagines his own “cage” breaking and feels briefly free; the window is liberating, while the room and its bed represent imprisonment.

Sitaram first courts Rukmini because she possesses both beauty and money. He borrows from her while disguising his need with teasing verses and flirtatious declarations, calling her his “Subhadra” and prompting her to supply increasingly intimate names for him. When she asks about interest, he dismisses the question as a joke, and after repeatedly borrowing, he simply forgets repayment. Their relationship then becomes secretive and conspiratorial, with Sitaram relying on her resources while treating her affection as something he can manipulate.

When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram turns on Rukmini, blaming her and threatening to burn her house, destroy her, and kill or free the Yubaraj. Rukmini realizes that Sitaram regards Udayaditya as his own concern and claims the same possessive right over him. Later, after helping stage the palace fire and believing Rukmini dead, Sitaram goes to her house intending to steal her money. Instead, he finds her alive, drenched, furious, and convinced that both he and Udayaditya must be destroyed. His feigned tenderness only intensifies her rage; she vows to make him pay, fetches a curved blade, and repeatedly strikes at the spot where he had stood. Sitaram abandons his bravado and escapes, realizing that Rukmini knows of the conspiracy and that the once-playful financial and romantic arrangement has become an openly murderous conflict.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a diversion: he helps loyalists ignite several rooms, obstructs the firefighting, and creates enough confusion for the guards to abandon Udayaditya’s cell. He then leads Udayaditya out and arranges his escape by boat with Basanta Ray.

The plan becomes a deliberate cover-up when Sitaram sets fire to the now-empty cell, plants bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword inside, and stages shouts suggesting that the prince is trapped and screaming. When the roof collapses, he encourages the guards to believe Udayaditya has died, while the planted remains and witnesses reinforce the story. He retrieves and destroys incriminating letters, takes the prince’s sword, and flees with his family, hoping the supposed death will conceal the escape. The deception works briefly, until Rukmini exposes the conspiracy and later reports confirm that Udayaditya reached Raigarh.

He takes Udayaditya’s rescue of him for granted, believing Udayaditya acted chiefly for his sister’s sake rather than out of concern for Ramchandra. He therefore feels no gratitude and later joins his courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya initially dismisses the Emperor of Delhi as an “empty fear,” insisting that the Emperor is not his god and that he will not be intimidated by the threat of imperial displeasure or its fifty thousand soldiers. His opponents then turn that very fear into a weapon: they forge a petition bearing Udayaditya’s seal, falsely presenting it as the prince’s complaint of treason against Pratapaditya to the Emperor, and have it delivered to the king as proof that his son is conspiring against him. Thus, the imperial threat he had scorned becomes the pretext for treating Udayaditya as a traitor and imprisoning him.

Vibha’s hair marks Surma’s intimate care and the emotional life of the palace. When Surma is present, Vibha secretly turns to her to have her hair arranged according to her own taste, making grooming a private bond between them, even as the Mahishi tries to impose her own style. After Surma’s disappearance, Vibha waits for her to braid her hair, but evening comes and it remains unbraided—a daily sign that Surma will not return. As the days pass, Vibha’s unkempt hair reflects the wider neglect and desolation of the palace, showing that Surma’s absence has left her without both personal care and emotional solace.
